newsitem.title: UK: Copper exports from FSU seen peaking in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Copper exports from FSU seen peaking in 1998.

text.p: Copper exports from the former Soviet Union are expected to peak in 1998 at 750,000 tonnes, then decline as domestic consumption picks up, Metal Bulletin Research said in a report.
Russian domestic demand has been falling at double-digit rates throughout most of the 1990s but it is expected to plateau this year, it added.

"Given the amount that copper consumption has fallen over the last few years, there is a large potential for a significant recovery," said the report, written as a joint project with CIS-based consultancy Infomine.
"Once consumption begins to bounce back, it will grow at a much faster rate than production, which is likely to be constrained by capacity," it added.

Although some end-use markets have disappeared and others are likely to use less copper-intensive material, significant growth potential remains with current consumption at less than one kg per person.
Copper ore deposits were extensively mapped by Soviet era geologists, with the bulk of explored reserves in Russia and Kazakhstan, but also in Uzbekistan, Armenia and more recently, in the Ukraine.
Additions to reserves, however, over the past few years has been minimal.
"The result is that the majority of proven reserves are fast being diminished at currently operating mines, several of which are likely to be exhausted by the turn of the century," the report said.
Total designed capacity of Russian refineries is about 900,000 tonnes per year, with output of 560,900 tonnes in 1996.
The Russian refineries, with some of the highest costs in the world, are vulnerable to a downturn in copper prices.
If this occurs, production at Urals-based plants could be cut, but Norilsk is unlikely to be much affected since it can write off copper losses against nickel and PGM earnings.
Tolling will remain important in the former Soviet Union, but substantial expansion is unlikely since an excess of global smelting capacity will come online over the next few years.
